parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking about what bandwidth tells you - it is about the range of frequencies an amplifier can handle, not about voltage size.
Hint 2: Now think what infinite would mean for that range - how would the gain behave at very low and very high frequencies?
parts.proper_answer: Infinite bandwidth means the voltage gain is the same for all frequencies of input signal.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What bandwidth really means**
Think of bandwidth as the range of input frequencies that get amplified properly. A real op-amp amplifies low frequencies well but its gain falls off at high frequencies.

Step 2: **Apply infinite to an ideal op-amp**
Infinite means there is no upper limit. So $$ \text{gain is constant for all frequencies} $$ The ratio $V_{OUT}/V_{IN}$ does not drop even for very high frequency signals.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
key_concepts: rate of change of output voltage
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the words slew rate - it is about how fast the output can change in time, measured in $\text{V s}^{-1}$.
Hint 2: Think about delay between input changing and output following - what would happen if there were zero delay?
parts.proper_answer: Infinite slew rate means the output voltage can change infinitely fast and follows any change in input voltage instantaneously with no time delay.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What slew rate measures**
Slew rate is the maximum rate of change of output voltage, $$ \text{slew rate} = \frac{\Delta V_{OUT}}{\Delta t} $$ A real op-amp takes a short time for its output to rise or fall.

Step 2: **Make it infinite for the ideal case**
Infinite means no speed limit. If the input jumps suddenly, the output jumps at exactly the same instant. There is no distortion or lag, even for rapidly changing signals.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Remember the name non-inverting - the input signal $V_{IN}$ must go to the non-inverting (+) input, not the (-) input.
Hint 2: Think about feedback for stability - a fraction of the output from the R1-R2 divider must be fed back to the inverting (-) input.
parts.proper_answer: Connect $V_{IN}$ to the + input. Connect the junction of $R_1$ and $R_2$ to the - input.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Place the input on the + terminal**
You are told this is a non-inverting amplifier, so the sign of the gain is positive. That only happens when the external signal goes into the $+$ terminal. Draw a wire from the $V_{IN}$ terminal on the left to the $+$ input of the triangle.

Step 2: **Close the negative feedback loop**
$R_1$ and $R_2$ form a potential divider between $V_{OUT}$ and 0 V. The voltage at their junction is a fraction of $V_{OUT}$. For negative feedback this sampled voltage must return to the $-$ input. Draw a wire from the $R_1$-$R_2$ junction to the $-$ input of the triangle.

parts.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Use the basic gain relation $V_{OUT} = \text{gain} \times V_{IN}$ and check whether the result lies within the $\pm 5.0\text{ V}$ supplies.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Multiply by the gain and check saturation**
For a non-inverting amplifier the gain is positive, so $$ V_{OUT} = G \times V_{IN} = 10 \times (-0.36\text{ V}) = -3.6\text{ V} $$ This is between $-5.0\text{ V}$ and $+5.0\text{ V}$, so the op-amp is not saturated and the full calculated value appears at the output.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Calculate $10 \times 0.56\text{ V}$ first, then ask yourself if an op-amp powered by $\pm 5.0\text{ V}$ can actually output that voltage.
parts.proper_answer: $V_{OUT} = +5.0\text{ V}$ (saturated at the positive supply rail).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot saturation**
The ideal calculation would give $$ V_{OUT} = 10 \times 0.56\text{ V} = 5.6\text{ V} $$ But the op-amp is powered between $+5.0\text{ V}$ and $-5.0\text{ V}$. The output can never go beyond the supply. So it saturates and sticks at approximately $+5.0\text{ V}$.
